text: The Great Dying is the name for the biggest extinction in the history of life. It happened about 252 million years ago, at the end of a time called the Permian, before the first dinosaurs. Somewhere around [[@percentages|80–90 percent]] of all kinds of sea animals died out, and about 70 percent of kinds of [[@lost-first-fish-land|land animals with backbones]].

The main suspect is a vast series of volcanic eruptions in what is now Siberia. They poured out [[lava|lava]] and gases for a very long time. The gases heated the planet, made the seas more acidic and stole oxygen from the water.

st.prompt: Roughly how many kinds of sea animals died out in the Great Dying?

options.t: About 8 or 9 in every 10
About 1 in every 10
About half

st.reveal: Most estimates say around 80–90 percent of sea species vanished, and some say more. By comparison, the extinction that ended the dinosaurs wiped out about three in every four species overall.

src: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Deep Time.

n.certNote: Scientists agree the extinction happened and that giant volcanic eruptions in Siberia were very likely the main cause. Exactly how the eruptions killed so much, and how fast, is still being worked out.

myth: The extinction that killed the dinosaurs was the worst in Earth's history.
It was the most famous, but not the worst. The Great Dying, about 186 million years earlier, killed a larger share of life in the sea and on land.

sec.t:
Before the Great Dying, almost all the land on Earth was joined into one supercontinent called [[@pangaea|Pangaea]]. India sat in its southern part, called [[gondwana|Gondwana]], next to Africa, [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] and Australia. Forests of strange seed plants grew there, and coal from those forests is mined in India today.

On land lived tusked plant-eaters and sabre-toothed hunters, many of them distant relatives of [[mammal|mammals]]. In the seas, there were reefs, sea lilies, fish, spiral-shelled animals and the last of the [[@trilobites|trilobites]], which had lived for about 270 million years.

Carbon dioxide traps heat, which is why it matters for [[@climate-change|climate change]] today. At the end of the Permian, temperatures shot up. Studies of [[fossil|fossil]] teeth suggest that [[tropical|tropical]] seas may have reached around 40°C at the surface, hot bath temperature, much too warm for most sea life.

Warm water holds less oxygen, so large parts of the ocean became hard to breathe in. Carbon dioxide also [[dissolve|dissolves]] in seawater and makes it more acidic, which makes it harder for animals to build shells. Reef-building animals were among the worst hit. Reefs almost vanished from the fossil record for millions of years. The corals that build today's [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] belong to a newer group that appeared afterwards.

A few kinds of animals were lucky or tough. The most famous is Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized plant-eater with two tusks and a beak, related to the ancestors of mammals. For a while after the extinction it was one of the commonest land animals on Earth. Its fossils have been found in South Africa, Antarctica, China and the Damodar valley in eastern India. Finding the same animal on lands now far apart helped show that the continents were once joined, as described in [[@india-drift|India's long journey]].

Life took millions of years to recover. For a long stretch after the extinction, there are almost no coal layers anywhere in the world, a sign that big forests had collapsed too. Even insects, which survive most disasters, suffered one of their worst losses ever. When life did bounce back, the world had changed. New groups of reptiles appeared, and among them, within about 20 million years, were the first dinosaurs.

text: Some cities are sinking because the ground beneath them is squashing down. This is called subsidence. Many big cities are built on soft layers of clay, silt and sand, laid down by old lakes, rivers and deltas. These layers are soaked with water, which helps hold them up.

When people pump that water out through wells to drink, farm and run factories, the layers squeeze together like a sponge being wrung out. The ground on top drops, slowly but steadily. Heavy buildings and roads add to the problem. Near the sea, the sinking makes floods much worse.

st.reveal: These cities stand on soft layers of clay and sand soaked with water. When wells pump that water out, the layers squash together like a drying sponge, and the ground on top drops.

sec.h: A city on an old lake
sec.t:
Mexico City is one of the fastest-sinking cities on Earth. It was built on the bed of a lake that the Aztecs once lived beside. About 2 crore people now live there, and much of their water is pumped from under the city.

Between October 2025 and January 2026, a new radar satellite called NISAR, built jointly by NASA and ISRO, measured parts of the city sinking more than 2 cm a month. That adds up to over 24 cm a year, close to the length of a school ruler. In the 1990s and 2000s, some areas were dropping even faster, around 35 cm a year. The Angel of Independence, a tall golden statue built in 1910, has needed 14 extra steps added to its base so people can still climb up to it.

There is good news. In the 1900s, parts of Tokyo sank by around 4 metres as factories pumped out groundwater. From the 1960s onwards, Japan passed laws limiting the pumping and brought in water from rivers and dams instead. The sinking slowed to almost nothing.

That shows the problem can be fixed. Once the soft layers are squashed, though, they rarely spring back. The land that was lost stays lost. So the sooner a city acts, the better. Venice shows the same story. In the 1900s, wells pumping water for nearby industry made the ground sink faster. Italy closed most of them in the 1970s, but the city still floods more often as the sea rises.

Buildings matter a little too. In 2023, scientists worked out that New York City's buildings weigh about 762 billion kg, as much as about 14 crore elephants. That weight helps press the city down by a millimetre or two a year in some places.

In India, Joshimath in Uttarakhand made news in 2023 when cracks spread through homes and roads as the hillside town sank. Experts blamed loose ground, water seeping underneath and heavy building. Studies have also found sinking in parts of Delhi, Kolkata and other cities where wells pull up lots of groundwater.

Sinking land and [[@sea-level-rise|rising seas]] together are a double trouble for coastal cities, which is why places like [[@venice|Venice]] now raise giant barriers against high tides. The Netherlands has lived below sea level for centuries, and its tricks with dikes and pumps are the story of [[@world-netherlands-water|Dutch water engineering]]. Underground, a different kind of collapse can happen in seconds instead of years. When the roof of a hidden cave gives way, the result is a [[@sinkholes|sinkhole]] big enough to swallow a car.

text: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and the Moon line up so that one blocks light from another.

In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on part of our planet. If you are in the very centre of that shadow, the Sun disappears completely for a few minutes. In a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow slides across the Moon, often turning it a deep coppery red.
Solar eclipses can only happen at new moon, and lunar eclipses only at full moon.

st.prompt: The Moon goes around Earth every month. Why don't we get a solar eclipse every month?

options.t: The Moon's path is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Sun
The Moon is too small most months
Clouds usually hide it

st.reveal: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees compared with Earth's path around the Sun. Most months the Moon's shadow misses Earth entirely. Only when everything lines up exactly do we get an eclipse.

d.try: In a dark room, use a torch as the Sun, a football as Earth and a small ball as the Moon. Move the small ball between the torch and the football and watch its shadow fall on the "Earth". Then move it behind the football into Earth's shadow to make a lunar eclipse.
myth: Food cooked or left out during an eclipse becomes harmful to eat.
The light reaching Earth during an eclipse is ordinary sunlight, just less of it. Food is not affected. The one real danger is looking straight at the Sun without proper eye protection.

sec.t:
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. It is also about 400 times farther away. So from Earth they look almost exactly the same size, and the Moon can cover [[@sun-what|the Sun]] like a coin covering a coin.

When it does, day turns to deep twilight. Stars and planets appear. Birds go quiet, and the temperature can drop by several degrees. Around the black disc of the Moon, the Sun's thin outer layer, the corona, glows in pale silvery streamers. It is normally invisible because the rest of the Sun is far too bright.

The Moon's shadow on Earth is narrow, usually less than a couple of hundred kilometres wide. That is why a total solar eclipse is only seen along a thin path, while people outside it see the Sun only partly covered.

During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon doesn't vanish. It glows a dull orange or red. That is because some sunlight bends through Earth's [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] on its way past. The air scatters away blue light, which is also why the [[@sky-blue|sky is blue]], and lets red light through.

So the red light on the Moon is the glow of every sunrise and sunset happening on Earth at that moment. Lunar eclipses are completely safe to watch. A total one was seen across India in September 2025.

On 18 August 1868, a total solar eclipse crossed India. The French [[astronomer|astronomer]] Jules Janssen set up his instruments at Guntur, in today's Andhra Pradesh. He split the light from the glowing gas around the Sun into its colours and saw a bright yellow line that no known [[element|element]] could explain.

The English astronomer Norman Lockyer later named the mystery element helium, after *helios*, the Greek word for the Sun. It was not found on Earth until 1895.

Eclipses helped science again in 1919. Astronomers photographed stars near the darkened Sun and showed that its [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] bends starlight, just as [[@einstein|Albert Einstein]] had predicted.

{{story:einstein}}

Never look straight at the Sun, even when most of it is covered. Its light can damage the back of your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] without any pain. [[@how-sunglasses|Ordinary sunglasses]] are nowhere near dark enough. Use certified eclipse glasses, or make a pinhole projector and look at the image on paper instead.

Eclipses have been watched with awe for thousands of years. In Hindu stories, the demon Rahu swallows the Sun or Moon, which soon slips free again. Ancient astronomers in Babylon, China and India learned to predict eclipses long before anyone knew why they happened.

On 8 April 2024, a total eclipse crossed Mexico, the United States and Canada. Millions of people stood outside in the sudden dusk and cheered when the Sun came back.

text: The universe has been growing since the [[@big-bang|Big Bang]], about 13.8 billion years ago. For most of the 20th century, scientists assumed that [[gravity|gravity]], pulling all the [[galaxy|galaxies]] towards each other, would slowly brake that growth.

In 1998, two teams of [[astronomer|astronomers]] checked. They were stunned. The growth wasn't slowing. It was speeding up, and had been for about the last 5 billion years. Something seems to push space apart, and it gets stronger relative to gravity as the universe grows. Scientists call this unknown something dark energy. It's one of the biggest unsolved puzzles in all of science.

st.prompt: In the 1990s, astronomers measured how fast the universe's expansion was changing. What did they expect to find?

options.t: That gravity was slowly braking the expansion
That the universe had stopped growing
That the universe was shrinking

st.reveal: Everyone expected gravity to slow things down, the way a ball thrown upwards slows. Instead, distant supernovae were dimmer than expected, which meant the expansion was speeding up. Something was pushing.

src: NASA Science, Dark Energy, Dark Matter.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, DESI results (2024 and 2025).
n.certNote: The speeding up is well measured, but nobody knows what causes it. "Dark energy" is a name for the mystery, not an explanation, and results from 2024 and 2025 hint that it may be changing over time.

d.try: Draw dots on a balloon with a marker, then blow it up slowly. Watch how every dot moves away from every other dot, and the dots far apart separate fastest. That's how galaxies move apart as space stretches. Now picture someone blowing harder and harder as time goes on.
myth: The universe is expanding into empty space outside it, like a bomb blast.
There is no "outside" that we know of. Space itself is stretching everywhere at once, carrying galaxies apart, rather than galaxies flying through empty space.

sec.t:
How do you measure the speed of the whole universe? The teams used a special kind of exploding star, a type Ia [[@supernova|supernova]]. These blasts all shine with nearly the same peak brightness, so they work like light bulbs of a known wattage. If one looks dim, it must be far away.

A single [[supernova|supernova]] can briefly outshine a whole galaxy of billions of stars. The teams found dozens of them, billions of [[@light-years|light-years]] away. They were dimmer than expected, so they were farther away than they should have been if the expansion were slowing. In 2011, Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery.

Back in 1917, [[@einstein|Albert Einstein]] added an extra term to his equations of gravity, called the cosmological constant. He wanted a universe that stayed still. When Edwin Hubble showed in 1929 that galaxies were rushing apart, Einstein dropped the idea.

Now the cosmological constant is back. The simplest explanation for dark energy is that empty space itself has a tiny amount of energy built in. As space stretches, there's more of it, so there's more push. But when physicists try to calculate how much energy empty space should have, their answer is wildly too big, by a factor with more than 100 zeros. Nobody knows why.

A new survey called DESI, on a telescope in Arizona, has mapped millions of galaxies in 3D. In 2024 and again in 2025, its results hinted that dark energy might be getting weaker over time. If true, that would mean it isn't a fixed property of space after all.

Scientists are careful here. The hints are not yet strong enough to count as a discovery. Upcoming telescopes, including Europe's Euclid and NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, should help.

The fate of the universe depends on dark energy. If it stays steady, [[@galaxies|galaxies]] will keep drifting apart until, in many billions of years, astronomers here would see only our own small neighbourhood of galaxies, with dark sky beyond. If it grows stronger, some scientists have suggested it could one day pull apart even [[atom|atoms]]. If it weakens, the universe might stop growing, or even shrink back. For now, it remains among the great [[@unsolved-problems|unsolved problems]], alongside puzzles that mathematicians have chased for centuries.

text: A peregrine falcon cruising through the air flies at about 65 to 90 km/h, fast for a bird but nothing record-breaking. Its secret is the dive, which falconers call a stoop. It climbs high above its prey, tucks in its wings and falls, steering as it goes. In a stoop it can pass 320 km/h, as fast as the quickest Shinkansen bullet trains.

In a famous experiment in 1999, a trained falcon named Frightful was released from a small plane and filmed diving at about 390 km/h. No other animal is known to move faster. That's why the peregrine is usually called the [[@fastest-animal|fastest animal]] on Earth.

st.prompt: How does a peregrine protect its eyes when diving at over 300 km/h?

options.t: A see-through third eyelid sweeps across each eye
It closes its eyes and dives blind
Its eyes sink deep into its skull

st.reveal: Like many birds, peregrines have a clear third eyelid called a nictitating membrane. It slides across the eye to keep it moist and clear of dust, while still letting the falcon see its target.

myth: The cheetah is the fastest animal in the world.
The cheetah is the fastest animal on land, at about 100–110 km/h in short bursts. A diving peregrine falcon is more than three times faster, which makes it the fastest animal of all.

sec.t:
At the top of a stoop, a peregrine folds its long, pointed wings tight against its body. Its shape becomes a smooth teardrop, which slips through the air with very little drag. [[@gravity-fall|Gravity]] does the rest, pulling it faster and faster.

Small adjustments of its wings and tail let it steer, even at full speed. It often strikes its prey, usually another bird, with its feet in mid-air, then swoops round to catch it as it falls.

sec.h: Breathing and seeing at top speed

sec.t:
In the middle of the 1900s, peregrine numbers crashed across North America and Europe. The cause was DDT, a [[pesticide|pesticide]] sprayed on farms. It built up in small birds, and then in the falcons that ate them. DDT made their eggshells so thin that they broke when the parents sat on them.

The USA banned most uses of DDT in 1972. Scientists bred peregrines in captivity and released young birds into the wild, sometimes from the roofs of tall buildings. The plan worked. In 1999 the peregrine was taken off the US [[endangered|endangered]] [[species|species]] list, one of conservation's great comebacks.

People have trained falcons to hunt for thousands of years, a sport called falconry. In the Arab world, India and Central Asia, peregrines and their relatives were prized by kings. Paintings from the Mughal court show emperors and nobles with hunting falcons perched on their gloved wrists.

Falcons now have modern jobs too. At some airports, trained falcons patrol the runways and scare away flocks of smaller birds that could be sucked into jet engines.

Peregrines naturally nest on high cliffs. To a peregrine, a skyscraper is just a cliff with windows, and the streets below are full of pigeons. Today they nest on buildings, bridges and church towers in cities like New York, London and Chicago, and some have live webcams that thousands of people watch.

The word peregrine means "wanderer", and northern peregrines fly thousands of kilometres to escape winter, some of them reaching India. India also has its own resident peregrine, the shaheen, which nests on cliffs and old forts. And the strangest part? A falcon in a stoop falls faster than a human skydiver, who tops out at around 200 km/h, as you'll see in the story of [[@sky-skydiving|skydiving]].

text: Corals turn white when the sea gets too warm for too long. A coral is an animal, but it lives in partnership with tiny [[algae|algae]] inside its body. The algae use sunlight to make food by [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] and share most of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives them shelter. The algae also give corals their browns, greens and golds.

When the water stays about 1 °C or more above its usual summer maximum for several weeks, this partnership breaks down. The coral pushes the algae out. Without them, its tissue becomes see-through, and you can see the white limestone skeleton underneath. That is bleaching.

st.prompt: A coral has turned completely white. What does that tell you?

options.t: It is stressed and starving, but may still recover
It has died and turned to stone
It is shedding its old skin to grow

st.reveal: White means the coral has pushed out the algae that feed it and give it colour, so you see its white skeleton through clear tissue. If the water cools within a few weeks, the algae can move back in. If the heat lasts too long, the coral starves.

sec.t:
Each coral is a colony of thousands of tiny animals called [[polyp|polyps]], each smaller than a pea. Their algae partners are so small that millions can fit in a patch of coral the size of a fingernail.

Scientists think heat makes the algae's food-making machinery go wrong. Instead of sugar, they start releasing harmful chemicals. The coral reacts by getting rid of them, much as you might drop a hot pan. It solves one problem but creates another, because the coral has lost its main supply of food.

A bleached coral can survive for a while on stored energy and by catching [[plankton|plankton]] with its [[tentacle|tentacles]]. If temperatures fall within a few weeks, the algae return and the colour comes back. If the heat lasts, the coral slowly starves.

{{story:photosynthesis}}

Small patches of bleaching have always happened. What changed is the scale. In 1998, a strong [[@el-nino|El Niño]] warmed oceans across the planet, and reefs bleached from the Caribbean to the Indian Ocean. More global events followed in 2010 and from 2014 to 2017. In April 2024, scientists at NOAA in the United States declared a fourth global bleaching event.

Australia's [[@great-barrier-reef|Great Barrier Reef]] has had several mass bleachings since 2016. In the summer of 2023, a [[@heatwaves|marine heatwave]] hit the reefs of the Florida Keys, and some shallow water near the coast felt as warm as a hot bath. Most scientists link the rising number of events to [[@climate-change|climate change]], as the oceans soak up extra heat.

India has coral reefs in four main places: the Gulf of Kachchh in Gujarat, the Gulf of Mannar between India and Sri Lanka, [[@india-wonder-andaman-reefs|the Andaman and Nicobar Islands]], and [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]]. India's reefs have bleached many times during marine heatwaves, with major events in 1998 and 2010.

For people on these islands, reefs are more than pretty scenery. They protect beaches from waves, feed fish that families eat and sell, and draw visitors. Researchers from Indian institutes dive regularly to count living and bleached corals, so they can see which reefs bounce back and which do not.

Satellites cannot see a single coral, but they can measure the temperature of the sea surface every day. NOAA's Coral Reef Watch adds up how many weeks a patch of ocean has stayed unusually warm. When the total climbs, reef managers get a warning that bleaching is likely, sometimes before divers see any white at all.

Some reefs seem tougher than others, and scientists are studying corals that survive heatwaves. They hope those tough corals hold clues for helping reefs through warmer decades ahead.

text: A tide pool is a pocket of seawater left behind among the rocks when the [[@tides|tide]] goes out. Rocky shores are full of them, from tiny cracks to pools big enough to wade into. Each one becomes a small world for a few hours, cut off from the open sea.

Many animals live there. [[@clownfish|Sea anemones]] open like flowers to catch food. Barnacles, mussels and limpets cling to the rocks. Snails graze on slimy films of [[algae|algae]]. [[@crabs|Crabs]] hide under stones, and small fish dart into cracks. You may find starfish, sea urchins, sea slugs and sometimes a small octopus. Seaweeds give shade and shelter. All of them must cope with a home that changes completely twice a day.

st.prompt: When the tide goes out, mussels and barnacles are left in the hot sun. How do they keep from drying out?

They dig deep into the rock
They swim to the nearest pool

st.reveal: Mussels pull their two shells tightly together, and barnacles close little plates over their opening. A small amount of seawater is sealed inside, keeping them moist until the tide comes back.

sec.t:
The shore between high and low tide is called the [[intertidal|intertidal]] zone. It is one of the toughest places on Earth to live. When the tide is in, animals are pounded by [[@waves-how|waves]]. When it goes out, they may bake in the sun or freeze on a cold night.

A tide pool can change fast. On a hot day, the water warms up, loses oxygen and gets saltier as it evaporates. When it rains, the pool gets less salty. Animals that live there must survive all of this until the sea comes back and refreshes the water.

Tide pools can be fierce places. Sea anemones are animals, cousins of [[@jellyfish-old|jellyfish]], and their soft [[tentacle|tentacles]] carry tiny stinging cells that catch passing shrimps and fish. Starfish crawl slowly over mussel beds and open them, as you can read in [[@starfish|how a starfish eats]].

Some crabs and small fish change colour to match the rocks. Octopuses sometimes hunt in larger pools and can squeeze through any gap bigger than their beak. Shore birds, such as herons and oystercatchers, visit at low tide to pick off anything they can find.

The best time to explore is at low tide, especially during spring tides, when the water goes out farthest. These happen around the new and full moon, as you can read in [[@moon-phases|Moon phases]]. Always go with an adult, check the tide times, and keep an eye on the sea, because waves and the returning tide can come in fast.

On the Pacific coast of the USA, places like Monterey in California are famous for their pools. In 1939, the marine [[biologist|biologist]] Ed Ricketts wrote a guidebook to them with Jack Calvin, called Between Pacific Tides, still read today. In India, groups in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] lead walks along the city's rocky shores at low tide, finding sea anemones, octopuses and [[@coral-reefs|corals]] right beside the busy city. Look closely, touch gently, and put back any stone you turn over.

text: Most lizards can't walk up a wall. The famous wall-climbers are geckos, including the small, pale house lizard that chirps "tik-tik-tik" near tube lights across India.

A gecko's toes look smooth, but under a [[microscope|microscope]] they are covered in ridges carrying hundreds of thousands of tiny hairs called setae. Each hair splits at the end into hundreds of even smaller flat tips, far thinner than a human hair.

Those tips get so close to the wall that a very weak attraction between [[molecule|molecules]], called the van der Waals force, kicks in. One tip on its own holds almost nothing. Billions of them together can hold the gecko's whole weight, even upside down.

myth: The common house lizard is poisonous, and food it falls into becomes deadly.
House geckos are not venomous. Like many animals, they can carry germs such as Salmonella, so it's sensible to throw away food they've touched and wash hands, but the lizard itself is not poison.

sec.t:
For a long time, people guessed that geckos used suction cups or some kind of glue. Neither is true. Their feet are dry and leave no sticky trace.

In 2000, a team led by the American [[biologist|biologist]] Kellar Autumn measured the pull of a single gecko hair for the first time. The result was tiny, but when they multiplied it by all the hairs on a foot, the numbers were huge. A gecko could, in theory, hang from a single toe.

The trick works on almost anything smooth: glass, painted walls, polished stone. It even works in a [[vacuum|vacuum]]. It fails on surfaces that attract nothing, like a non-stick pan, and it weakens when the feet are wet.

Sticking is only half the problem. A gecko racing after a moth has to unstick each foot in a split second, many times a second.

It does this by peeling, not pulling. Geckos curl their toes up from the tip, like peeling sticky tape off a parcel. Changing the angle of the hairs breaks their grip almost instantly. Then the toe uncurls and slaps down again.

Geckos also keep their feet clean without washing. Dirt particles stick to the wall more strongly than to the tiny hairs, so a few steps rub them off.

{{story:robots}}

There are more than 7,000 kinds of lizard, and they live in very different ways. Monitor lizards climb trees with sharp claws. The garden lizard you see bobbing its head on Indian walls, with a red throat in the breeding season, uses claws too. Many desert lizards never climb at all.

Even among geckos, not all have sticky pads. The leopard gecko, a popular pet in the USA, has small claws instead. Anoles, the little green lizards of Florida and the Caribbean, grew pads of their own separately.

The Indian house gecko spends its nights near lights, waiting for insects. A single lizard can eat a lot of mosquitoes, moths and flies. Many families are glad to have one, even if they jump when it falls off the ceiling. House geckos are most active at night, and their big eyes see well in dim light. During the day they hide in cracks, behind cupboards and under roof tiles.

If you grab a house gecko, it may drop its tail. The tail keeps wriggling to distract a [[predator|predator]] while the lizard escapes. A new, slightly shorter tail grows back over a few weeks.

Engineers have copied gecko feet to make dry tapes that grip and release cleanly. Stanford University built a climbing [[@robots|robot]] called Stickybot, and NASA engineers have tested gecko-style grippers for catching objects in space, where ordinary suction doesn't work. It's a lesson in [[@friction|friction]] and stickiness written into the toes of an animal that also has to [[@camouflage|hide]] from hungry birds.

text: A microwave oven fills its metal box with invisible waves called microwaves. They are part of the same family as [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] and light, but far too long to see: each wave is about 12 centimetres from peak to peak.

Most food contains water, and each water [[molecule|molecule]] is slightly lopsided. One end carries a small positive electric charge and the other a small negative one. Microwaves make the electric field in the oven swing back and forth about 2.45 billion times a second. Every time it swings, the water molecules twist to line up with it. All that twisting and bumping into neighbouring molecules turns into heat, a bit like rubbing your hands together to warm them. The hot water then heats the rest of the food. Dry things, like a plain paper napkin or an empty glass bowl, warm up much less. Ice warms surprisingly slowly too, because the molecules in frozen water are locked in place and can't twist freely.

st.prompt: Why does a microwave oven heat soup much more than the bowl it sits in?

The bowl reflects all the heat back

st.reveal: Water molecules are lopsided, with one end slightly positive and the other slightly negative. The microwaves flip them back and forth billions of times a second, and that jostling heats the food. Many dry bowls have little water, so they warm up mostly from the hot food inside.

myth: Microwave ovens cook food from the inside out.

Microwaves only reach a few centimetres into food. They heat the outer layer first, and the heat then spreads slowly inward. That is why a thick piece of food can be hot outside and cold in the middle, and why it helps to stir.

sec.t:
Inside the oven, microwaves bounce off the metal walls. Where waves overlap, some spots get strong waves and others get almost none. So a plate standing still would cook unevenly, with hot spots and cold spots a few centimetres apart.

That's why most microwaves have a turning plate, and why instructions say to stir halfway through. Without a turntable, the hot spots in a sheet of melted cheese or chocolate are spaced about 6 centimetres apart, half the length of one wave.

The front door has a metal mesh with tiny holes, a millimetre or two wide. Light, with its very short waves, passes through, so you can watch your food. Microwaves are far too long to fit, so they bounce back inside. When the door opens, a safety switch shuts the magnetron off at once.

Metal objects inside can cause sparks, especially foil with crinkled edges or forks with points. The waves push electric charges in the metal, which bunch up at sharp tips and jump across the air. Ceramic, glass and many plastics let the waves pass straight through.

Microwaves don't make food [[radioactive|radioactive]]. They stop the instant the oven switches off, and nothing lingers in the food. The heated food is just hot, the same as food warmed on a stove.

Microwaves in an oven also have a lot in common with [[@wifi|Wi-Fi]], which uses waves of a very similar length. A leaky old oven can sometimes make Wi-Fi stutter while it runs. Today microwave ovens sit in [[@kitchens-history|kitchens]] across the USA and in many Indian homes and offices, warming up rice, dal and leftover [[@cooking-science|cooking]] in a couple of minutes.

text: Kathak began with storytellers. In northern India, travelling performers called *kathakars* acted out stories from the epics, especially tales of Krishna, with songs, gestures and steps. Over the centuries, the dance moved from temples and village squares into royal courts.

There it picked up speed, flair and new costumes. Today Kathak is known for dazzling footwork, called *tatkar*, and long sequences of spins, called *chakkars*. Unlike Bharatanatyam's deep bent-knee position, Kathak is danced mostly upright, with straight legs, and the dancer's feet beat out [[@rhythm-beat|rhythms]] like a drum.

options.t: They fix their eyes on one spot and turn their head round last
They close their eyes while spinning

st.reveal: This trick is called spotting. Keeping the eyes on one point for as long as possible, then snapping the head round, gives the balance organs in the inner ear less confusing movement to deal with.

myth: Kathak was invented in the Mughal court.
Kathak grew from older traditions of storytellers, called kathakars, who acted out tales from the epics. Mughal and other royal courts later changed its costumes, music and style.

sec.t:
A Kathak performance mixes pure dance with storytelling. In a storytelling piece, the dancer might show Radha waiting for Krishna, or Krishna teasing the village girls by the river. The dancer uses gestures and the face, often gentler and more natural than in southern styles.

Then the [[rhythm|rhythm]] takes over. The dancer recites strings of rhythm [[syllable|syllables]], called *bols*, like "ta thei thei tat", and then dances exactly what was spoken. The last spin often lands on *sam*, the first beat of the rhythm cycle, with a sudden stop that makes audiences gasp.

A Kathak dancer wears *ghungroo*, strings of brass bells tied around each ankle. Experienced dancers often wear over a hundred bells on each foot. By changing how the heel and toes strike the floor, dancers can play soft, fast or thunderous patterns.

The dancer often "talks" with a [[@tabla|tabla]] player. The drummer plays a pattern, and the dancer copies it with the feet, or the other way round. These playful exchanges can go faster and faster until the audience laughs and claps along.

sec.h: Why the spins don't topple them
sec.t:
Spinning makes most people dizzy because fluid in the inner ear keeps sloshing after you stop, as you can read in [[@ears-hear|how ears work]]. [[@brain-works|The brain]] gets mixed messages from the eyes and the ears.

Kathak dancers use spotting. They keep their eyes on a fixed point, then whip the head round quickly to find it again. Years of practice also seem to train the brain to pay less attention to the confusing signals. A strong dancer can finish dozens of spins and still hold a pose without wobbling.

In the 1900s, Kathak teachers moved from royal courts to schools and stages. One of the best known was Birju Maharaj of the Lucknow gharana, who taught generations of students and [[@bollywood-dance|choreographed dances for films]].

Hindi cinema loved Kathak. Many classic [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] films feature Kathak-style dances with swirling skirts and spins. Today Kathak is taught in cities from Delhi to New York, and some dancers mix it with flamenco, the Spanish dance, which also uses stamping feet and sharp turns.

text: Modern [[architecture|architecture]] is a style that grew in the early 1900s. Its [[@jobs-architect|architects]] wanted buildings to be honest about what they were made of and what they were for. They used new materials like steel, reinforced concrete and large sheets of [[@glass-made|glass]], and they removed most decoration.

A modern building usually has flat roofs, clean lines, open spaces inside and big windows. Its shape comes from its use. An American architect, Louis Sullivan, summed this up in 1896 with a phrase that became famous: "form follows function".

st.reveal: Nobody wants to climb 20 floors of stairs. In the 1850s, Elisha Otis showed a lift with a brake that caught it if the rope snapped. Together with steel frames, safe lifts made skyscrapers possible.

myth: Modern architecture means any building that is new.

Modern architecture is a particular style and set of ideas from roughly the 1900s to the 1970s. A building put up last year might copy an old style, while a modernist house can be nearly a hundred years old.

sec.t:
For thousands of years big buildings stood up on thick walls of stone or brick. The walls carried all the weight, so the taller the building, the thicker the walls at the bottom.

In the 1800s, factories began making strong iron and then steel. Engineers learned to build a skeleton frame of steel beams, like the bones of a body, which carried the weight instead. Walls became thin skins that could even be made of glass. Reinforced concrete, concrete with steel rods inside, could be poured into almost any shape. Iron structures like the [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] showed how strong and light a frame could be.

sec.h: The Bauhaus and the glass box
sec.t:
In 1919 the architect Walter Gropius founded a school in Germany called the Bauhaus. It taught that art, craft and industry should work together, and that good design should be simple, useful and affordable. Its teachers designed buildings, furniture, lamps and even typefaces.

Many Bauhaus teachers later moved to the United States. One, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, became known for elegant glass and steel towers. He is often linked with the phrase "less is more", which summed up the modern love of simplicity.

After independence, India's leaders wanted buildings that looked towards the future. Prime Minister [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]] invited Le Corbusier to design much of [[@chandigarh|Chandigarh]], the new capital of [[@punjab|Punjab]], in the 1950s. Its concrete government buildings, with bold shapes and deep shadows, are now a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

Indian architects then made modern architecture their own. [[@indian-architecture-modern|Balkrishna Doshi]], who had worked with Le Corbusier, designed low-cost housing and campuses that suit India's heat and [[monsoon|monsoon]]. In 2018 he became the first Indian to win the Pritzker Prize, architecture's top award. Laurie Baker, a British-born architect who settled in Kerala, built cheap, cool homes from local brick with clever gaps that let in air and light.

Modern architecture changed cities everywhere. Its supporters say it gave people cleaner, brighter homes and offices, and it could be built fast for growing cities. Its critics say some modern buildings feel cold and grey, and that rows of identical concrete blocks made neighbourhoods dull.

Later architects mixed modern ideas with colour, curves and local traditions. The [[@lotus|Lotus Temple]] in [[@delhi|Delhi]], opened in 1986, uses concrete covered in white marble to form 27 petals. Like many of the best [[@design-everyday|designers of everyday things]], its architects began with a simple question: what is this building for?

text: Dashrath Manjhi cut through the mountain with a hammer, a chisel and a crowbar. He did it alone, a few chips at a time, from around 1960 to 1982.

The result is a gap through a rocky ridge near his village, Gehlaur, in Bihar's Gaya district. It is about 110 m long, roughly the length of a football field, and about 9 m wide. In places it slices almost 8 m down into the rock, which is as deep as a two-storey house is tall. People in India now call him the Mountain Man.

st.reveal: Before the path, villagers had to walk around the ridge. Most accounts give about 55 km for the old route and about 15 km after Manjhi's cut, though figures vary a little.

myth: Dashrath Manjhi dug a tunnel through the mountain.
He cut an open path, more like a deep trench or gap through the top of a rocky ridge. You walk through it under the open sky, with rock walls on both sides.

sec.t:
Gehlaur sat on one side of a long ridge of the Gehlour hills. Schools, markets and the nearest hospital were on the other side, near the town of Wazirganj. To reach them, people either climbed a narrow, dangerous track over the top or walked the long way round.

Manjhi belonged to the Musahar community, one of the poorest groups in Bihar. He worked as a labourer, often breaking stone and digging for others. So he knew how [[@rocks-types|rock]] cracks and where it is weak.

At first, villagers called him mad. He worked in the early morning and after his paid jobs, in the burning summer and the cold winter. A crowbar let him prise loose big slabs, the same idea as using a [[@lever-lift|lever]] to lift a heavy box. The chisel did the rest.

There were no explosives and no machines. Picture moving a pile of rock bigger than a school bus, then doing it again, and again, hundreds of times. Slowly, a gap opened. Some villagers began to bring him food and help.

By 1982, the path was finished. The walk to Wazirganj that used to take most of a day could now be done in a couple of hours.

Manjhi kept pushing for a proper road and other help for his village. He once walked to Delhi, mostly along the railway line, to take his request to the government. That is more than 1,000 km.

Officials were slow. Manjhi died in 2007, and a proper paved road through his cut came only years later. It is now known as the Dashrath Manjhi Path. India Post issued a stamp in his honour in 2016, and a Hindi film, *Manjhi: The Mountain Man*, told his story in 2015.

Modern [[@tunnels|tunnel]] machines can chew through rock at several metres a day. Manjhi managed a few centimetres. What he lacked in power he made up for in years.

Today, visitors come to Gehlaur to walk through the gap and touch the chisel marks still visible on its walls. A memorial to Manjhi stands close to the path he cut. Children from Gehlaur now take the short way to schools and markets their grandparents could reach only after a long, hot walk around the hills.

His story is often told alongside another Indian who refused to give up. Jadav Payeng planted trees on a bare sandbank in the Brahmaputra for decades, until the [[@india-forest-man|Forest Man]] had grown a jungle big enough for elephants and tigers.

text: Algebra is the part of maths where you use a letter or symbol to stand for a number you don't know yet. Instead of saying "some number plus 7 makes 12", you write x + 7 = 12. Then you use rules to find x, which here is 5.

That might sound like a small trick, but it changed maths. With letters, you can describe patterns that work for every number at once, and solve problems that would be very hard in words alone. Algebra grew over thousands of years, with important steps in [[@babylon|Babylon]], Greece, India, Baghdad and Europe.

sec.t:
Around 820 CE, a scholar named Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad, at a famous centre of learning called the House of Wisdom, one of the [[@great-libraries|great libraries]] of its time. He wrote a book on solving problems, with a title that included the words *al-jabr* and *al-muqabala*.

*Al-jabr* means restoring or reuniting broken parts. In maths, it meant moving a subtracted amount to the other side of an equation to make it whole again. Europeans who translated the book turned *al-jabr* into "algebra". His own name, al-Khwarizmi, gave us another word: [[@algorithms|algorithm]].

His book had no x or y. Everything was written in words, even the numbers. He called the unknown *shay*, meaning "thing", and showed step by step how to balance and simplify problems so the thing could be found. Problems were about real things, such as sharing out land or money among family members.

For centuries, most algebra was written in long sentences. Symbols arrived slowly. In the late 1500s, the French mathematician François Viète used letters for both unknown and known numbers. Then, in 1637, René Descartes used letters from the end of the alphabet, especially x, y and z, for unknowns, and letters from the start for known amounts.

His habit stuck. Nobody is quite sure why x became the favourite. One popular story says printers had plenty of spare x's, but there is no good evidence for it.

Algebra is everywhere once you look. A shopkeeper working out how many packets fit in a box is doing it. A game designer uses it to make a character jump in a smooth curve. A [[@programming|programmer]] writes it into almost every line of code, using names like "score" or "speed" for numbers that change.

Scientists use algebra to write the laws of nature in short form. [[@einstein|Einstein]]'s E = mc² is algebra: three letters that describe how much energy is locked inside matter. It took centuries of mathematicians writing in long sentences to make a line that short possible.

text: India counts in lakhs and crores: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 and 1 crore = 1,00,00,000.
Much of the world counts in thousands, millions and billions: 1 lakh is a hundred thousand, and 1 crore is 10 million. So 100 crore make a billion.

The numbers are the same. Only the names and the commas change. The trouble is that our brains are bad at feeling the difference between big numbers. A crore and a billion both just sound like "a lot". Turning them into time, distance or rice grains helps.

A billion is a thousand times bigger. A million seconds is about 11 and a half days. A billion seconds is about 32 years.

sec.t:
Write ten million the Indian way and you get 1,00,00,000. Write it the international way and you get 10,000,000. After the first three digits, the Indian system puts a comma every two digits. The international system puts one every three.

Each system matches its names. Indian names jump by a hundred: thousand, lakh, crore. International names jump by a thousand: thousand, million, billion. Older Indian names go further, with arab for 100 crore and kharab for 10,000 crore, though few people use them now. The words are old too: *lakh* comes from the [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] *laksha*, and *crore* from *koti*.

India has about 140 crore people, and the USA about 34 crore, according to recent estimates. Together, that is more than one in every five humans on Earth. The whole world's [[@population|population]] passed 800 crore (8 billion) in 2022.

Go bigger and the numbers stop being about people. Our [[galaxy|galaxy]] may hold between 100 and 400 billion stars, so [[astronomer|astronomers]] measure space in [[@light-years|light years]] instead of kilometres. Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old, a number geologists squeeze into a single day to make it feel real in [[@earth-age|Earth's age]].

Scientists who study how children learn maths have found that most of us picture numbers on a mental line. Small numbers get lots of space, and big ones get squashed together at the far end. That is why a crore and a billion can feel almost the same.

One fix is to use a ruler. If one lakh were a single millimetre, a crore would be 10 centimetres, about the width of your palm. A billion would be 10 metres, about the length of a school bus. The step from a crore to a billion is a hundred palms, not one.

Until 1974, a "billion" in Britain meant a million million, the number Americans call a [[@large-numbers-names|trillion]]. Many European languages still use it that way. Britain's government switched to the American meaning, and most English speakers followed.

Ancient Indian thinkers loved huge numbers. A Buddhist text called the *Lalitavistara* tells of the young Siddhartha, later [[@buddha|the Buddha]], naming numbers far past a crore, up to a 1 followed by 53 zeros. Nobody needed such a number for shopping or counting cattle. People invented it because they enjoyed thinking about it.

text: Start with one grain on the first square, then keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. By the 64th and last square, the total comes to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains. That is about 18 billion billion.

A grain of [[@rice|rice]] weighs roughly 25 milligrams. So the full board would hold about 460 billion tonnes, a pile far bigger than any mountain range of grain anyone has seen. sec.h: The king and the clever player
sec.t:
The puzzle comes from an old legend. A wise man invents the game of [[@chess-india|chess]] and shows it to a king. The delighted king offers any reward. The inventor asks only for rice: one grain on the first square, doubling on each square after. The king laughs at such a small request, until his treasurers try to count it out.

Chess itself grew from an Indian game called chaturanga, played about 1,500 years ago. The story was told by [[medieval|medieval]] writers in Persia and the Arab world. In Kerala, there is an Indian version. Lord Krishna, disguised as a sage, plays chess with a king and asks for rice. When the king cannot pay, Krishna says the debt can be paid slowly, by serving rice pudding to pilgrims. People say that is why the Ambalappuzha temple serves sweet paal payasam to this day.

The odd thing about doubling is how gentle it looks at first. The whole first row of eight squares needs only 255 grains, about a pinch, weighing less than 7 grams. After two rows, you need 65,535 grains, still less than 2 kg, a small bag from the shop.

Then it speeds up. Square 21 alone holds about a million grains, a 25 kg sack. After 32 squares, halfway across the board, the running total is over 4 billion grains, about 107 tonnes, enough to fill several lorries.

The last square holds as much as all the other 63 squares put together, plus one grain. Laid end to end, the board's grains would stretch more than 10 [[lightyear|light-years]], far past the nearest star beyond the Sun.

{{story:kerala}}

Mathematicians write doubling with [[@exponents|exponents]]. Two multiplied by itself 10 times is 2 to the power 10, which equals 1,024. Square number n holds 2 to the power (n minus 1) grains. The total for the board is 2 to the power 64, minus 1.

Computers love this number. They count in [[@binary-code|binary]], using only 0s and 1s, and a 64-bit computer can store any whole number up to 2 to the power 64, minus 1. That is exactly the chessboard total. So the phone in your pocket can hold the king's debt in one tiny slot of its memory.

Doubling is also called exponential growth, and it shows up in surprising places. [[bacteria|Bacteria]] in a warm dish can double every 20 minutes or so, which is why food left out spoils so quickly. Money left in a bank grows in a similar way, as interest earns more interest. Bankers call it [[@maths-money-compound|compound interest]].

Our brains are bad at guessing doubling, because almost nothing in daily life grows that way. We expect things to add up, not multiply. The king made exactly that mistake. And doubling has an even stranger trick: fold a sheet of paper in half again and again, and in theory the [[@puzzle-folding-paper-moon|folds would reach the Moon]] faster than you would ever guess.

text: A cartoon is a series of still pictures shown so quickly that your brain sees them move. In cinema that means 24 pictures, called frames, every second. Hand-drawn cartoons often use 12 to 24 drawings for each second, with each drawing slightly different from the one before.

That adds up fast. A short cartoon can need thousands of drawings and many artists, and a feature film far more. Today many cartoons are made on computers, but the idea is the same: someone has to plan every movement, one frame at a time.
India has a growing animation industry, making cartoons for TV channels and films around the world, with large studios in cities such as Mumbai, Hyderabad and Bengaluru.

sec.t:
Every cartoon starts with a story. Artists sketch a storyboard, a comic strip of the whole film, to plan each scene and camera angle. Then [[@pop-cartoon-voices|voice actors]] usually record the lines, so animators can match mouths to words.

Lead animators draw the key poses, the most important moments of a movement: a cat crouching, then a cat in mid-leap. Assistants add the in-between drawings that fill the gaps. In the old days, the finished drawings were traced onto clear [[@plastic-made|plastic]] sheets called cels, painted by hand and photographed one by one over painted backgrounds.

sec.h: Tricks that bring drawings to life

sec.t:
In 1995, *Toy Story* became the first feature film made entirely with computer animation. Instead of drawing, artists build each character as a 3D model, a digital puppet with hundreds of controls for its arms, face and eyes. Animators pose the puppet at key moments, and the computer works out the movement in between.

Then comes rendering, when computers calculate light, shadow and colour for every frame. Each picture is stored as millions of [[@pixels|pixels]], and a single frame of a big film can take hours to render. Studios use rooms full of computers, called render farms, working day and night.

Some films use stop-motion. Animators move clay figures or puppets a tiny bit, take a photo, move them again and take another photo. A good day's work might produce only a few seconds of film.

Other studios use motion capture. Actors wear suits covered in markers, and cameras record their movements so they can be copied onto digital characters.

[[@indian-animation|Indian animation]] has a long history. In 1974, the government's Films Division made *Ek Anek Aur Ekta*, a short cartoon about unity that many Indians remember from TV. Today, Indian studios make series watched in many countries.

*[[@chhota-bheem|Chhota Bheem]]*, made by Green Gold Animation in Hyderabad, began on TV in 2008 and became one of the most popular children's [[@cartoon-network-india|cartoons in India]]. Indian artists also work on [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] films, doing everything from lighting to [[@perspective|perspective]] drawing for backgrounds. A cartoon you watch might have been coloured in Mumbai and animated in California.

text: Holi is a Hindu spring festival celebrated on the full moon of the month of Phalguna, usually in March. People throw coloured powder called gulal and spray coloured water at friends, family and strangers. For one day, almost everyone ends up pink, green and yellow.

The colours have several meanings. Many people link them to the god Krishna, who in popular stories playfully coloured Radha and the cowherd girls of Braj. Holi also celebrates the end of winter, when fields turn green and trees burst into flower. And on Holi, rich and poor, young and old, all get coloured the same.

The first day the temperature passes 30°C

st.reveal: Holi follows a lunar calendar, so it is held on the full moon of Phalguna. On the ordinary calendar, that falls anywhere from late February to late March.

sec.t:
The night before Holi, people light bonfires called Holika Dahan. The story behind it comes from Hindu tradition. A demon king named Hiranyakashipu wanted everyone to worship him. His son Prahlad stayed devoted to the god Vishnu.

The king's sister Holika had a cloak, or in some tellings a boon, that kept her safe from fire. She sat in a fire with Prahlad on her lap to kill him. Instead, the story says, Holika burned and Prahlad walked out unharmed. The bonfire marks the victory of good over evil, and families often roast new grain in it.

Traditional Holi colours came from plants. The orange flowers of the palash tree, also called tesu, were soaked in water to make a bright orange dye. [[@turmeric|Turmeric]] gave yellow, beetroot and hibiscus gave pink and red, and henna leaves gave green.

Today most powders are made in factories. Some contain harsh chemicals that can hurt [[@skin|skin]] and eyes. Many families have gone back to [[@crayons-paints|herbal colours]], and some cities sell colours made from flowers collected from temples. Oiling your hair and skin before playing makes colour easier to wash off.

Holi looks different in different places. In West Bengal, it is called Dol Jatra or Basanta Utsav, and people sing and wear yellow. In Punjab, Sikhs celebrate Hola Mohalla the day after Holi, with displays of martial arts and horse riding. Sweets such as gujiya, filled with sweet khoya and nuts, and the cold milk drink thandai are part of the day almost everywhere.

Holi is also a public holiday in [[@nepal|Nepal]]. Indian communities in the USA, the UK, Mauritius, Guyana and Fiji celebrate it too. In American cities, "Festival of Colors" events draw people of many backgrounds, and colour runs, races where runners are showered with powder, borrowed the idea.

For one day, Holi turns ordinary life upside down. Children can splash their teachers, and neighbours who have quarrelled are expected to make up. The saying "Bura na mano, Holi hai", meaning "Don't be offended, it's Holi", sums up the mood. It's also a reminder to play kindly. Not everyone wants to be soaked, and a quick "Can I?" before colouring someone keeps the fun fair. Like [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]], it ends with sweets shared between houses.

text: Vegetables often taste better as you grow up for a mix of reasons. Young children are naturally more sensitive to bitterness and more cautious about new foods. Many vegetables, like karela, methi, broccoli and cabbage, contain bitter chemicals that put them off.

As you grow, you taste these foods again and again. Your brain learns they are safe, and you start to notice other flavours, like sweetness, crunch and the taste of spices. Your [[gene|genes]] matter too. Some people taste bitterness far more strongly than others, all their lives.

st.reveal: Many poisonous plants taste bitter. Scientists think young children's strong dislike of bitterness may have helped protect them when they began exploring food. As we learn which bitter foods are safe, we start to accept them.

sec.h: A safety system on your tongue
sec.t:
Your tongue has thousands of taste buds, each with tiny cells that detect five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, a savoury taste found in tomatoes and cheese. Sweet usually means energy, and babies love it from birth. Bitter can be a warning, since many poisonous plants taste bitter.

Scientists think young children's strong dislike of bitterness helped keep them safe. A toddler who spat out bitter leaves was less likely to eat something harmful. The same instinct makes many children wrinkle their noses at karela, even though it is perfectly safe.

Taste learning starts very early. Flavours from a mother's food reach the fluid around a baby in the womb and later the breast milk. In a study at the Monell Chemical Senses Center in the USA, babies whose mothers drank carrot juice during pregnancy or breastfeeding made fewer disgusted faces when fed carrot-flavoured cereal.

That may be one reason children in different countries grow up loving different foods. A child in Andhra Pradesh may enjoy fiery chillies from early on. A child in Minnesota might prefer milder food. Both are learning from what their families eat.

About one in four people are so-called supertasters. They have a version of a gene that makes certain bitter chemicals taste extra strong. To them, broccoli, black coffee and some greens can taste harsh their whole lives. Others barely notice those flavours at all.

Taste cells are replaced every week or two, and the number of taste buds slowly falls as people get much older. Smell also changes. Since most flavour actually comes from smell, as the [[@taste-smell-link|taste and smell link]] shows, older people may find food tastes milder.

The vegetables have changed too. In the 1990s, Dutch scientists identified the bitter chemicals in Brussels sprouts. Plant breeders then grew milder varieties, and sales went up. Some foods are bitter on purpose, though. Karela is loved across India for its sharpness, cooked with onions, jaggery or spices to balance it. And the [[@tongue-taste|tongue]] has one more surprise: the old map showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back is wrong, since every part can taste every flavour. Umami, the savoury fifth taste hidden in tomatoes and cheese, has its own odd history in [[@food-science-umami|umami science]].

text: 5G is the fifth generation of mobile phone networks. Like 4G before it, it carries calls and internet data between your phone and nearby towers using [[@radio-waves|radio waves]]. The difference is that 5G can carry much more data at once, and with a much shorter delay.

On a good 5G connection, a full film can download in under a minute. In everyday use, speeds are usually a few hundred megabits per second, several times faster than typical 4G, though it depends a lot on where you are. 5G networks launched in South Korea and the United States in April 2019, and in India on 1 October 2022.

st.reveal: Higher-frequency waves can carry more data, but they fade quickly and struggle to pass through buildings. So networks using them need many small antennas close together, often on lamp posts and rooftops.

sec.t:
Speed is how much data arrives each second. Latency is how long the first bit takes to arrive after you ask for it. On 4G that delay is often a few tens of thousandths of a second. On 5G it can drop to just a few.

That sounds tiny, but it matters for things that must react instantly. A doctor guiding a robot from far away, or a car swapping warnings with the car ahead, can't afford to wait. People hope low latency will help [[@self-driving|self-driving cars]] and remote-controlled machines, though many of these uses are still being tested.

Radio waves come in different [[frequency|frequencies]]. 5G uses three main bands. Low frequencies travel far and pass through walls, but carry less data. Middle frequencies, the main band used in India, give a good balance. The highest frequencies, called millimetre waves because their [[wavelength|wavelength]] is only a few millimetres, carry huge amounts of data but fade within a few hundred metres.

Those short waves are stopped by walls, leaves and even heavy rain. So 5G networks use many small antennas, sometimes on lamp posts or bus stops. They also use antennas with dozens of tiny [[element|elements]] that aim a beam straight at your phone, a little like a torch instead of a bare bulb.

During the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], false rumours claimed 5G spread the virus. In Britain, some phone masts were even set on fire. Radio waves can't carry viruses. 5G uses non-ionising waves, which don't have enough energy to damage the DNA in cells, unlike [[@x-rays|X-rays]].

The World Health Organization says that, after much research, no harm to health has been linked to exposure from wireless technologies within international safety limits. Scientists keep studying the higher frequencies as networks grow.

In big Indian cities, 5G spread very quickly after 2022, as companies put up hundreds of thousands of new 5G antennas within two years. In rural areas of both India and the United States, many people still rely on 4G. Most phones switch back and forth without you noticing. The little "5G" at the top of the screen tells you which kind of tower your phone is talking to at that moment.

text: The bicycle was invented in stages over about 70 years. In 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais built a wooden two-wheeled "running machine". It had a seat and handlebars but no pedals. Riders pushed off the ground with their feet and coasted.

In the 1860s, French makers added pedals to the front wheel. In the 1870s came the tall penny-farthing. Then in 1885, an English inventor, John Kemp Starley, built the Rover, with two wheels of the same size and a chain driving the back wheel. That design, with air-filled [[@tyres|tyres]] added soon after, is still the basic bicycle you ride today.

st.reveal: With pedals attached straight to the front wheel, one turn of the pedals meant one turn of the wheel. A giant wheel covered more ground per push, so it was faster. The rider sat high up, though, and falls headfirst were common and painful.

sec.t:
Karl Drais lived in Mannheim, in what is now [[@germany|Germany]]. On 12 June 1817, he rode his running machine about 13 km, there and back, in a little over an hour, faster than walking. People called it a "dandy horse" or "hobby horse".

Some historians think Drais was looking for a way to travel without horses. In 1815, a huge volcanic eruption at Mount Tambora in Indonesia threw ash high into the sky. The next year was so cold in Europe that it was called the Year Without a Summer. Crops failed and horses were costly to feed. Whether this inspired Drais is debated, but it is a striking link between a [[@volcano|volcano]] and a vehicle.

In the 1860s, French makers fixed pedals and cranks to the front wheel. These iron-tyred bikes rattled so hard on cobbled streets that English riders called them boneshakers.

Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, a bigger front wheel meant more speed. So front wheels grew, until some were as tall as a grown man's shoulder. These were penny-farthings, named after a large British penny coin and a small farthing coin. They were fast, but the rider sat so high that hitting a stone could send him flying over the handlebars.

Bicycles changed lives. Workers could live further from factories. Women in particular found new freedom. They could travel alone, and many switched from long skirts to looser clothes for riding. The American campaigner [[@susan-b-anthony|Susan B. Anthony]] said in 1896 that the bicycle had done more for women's freedom than almost anything else, at a time when women were fighting for the [[@womens-vote|vote]].

Bicycle shops became workshops for inventors. In Dayton, Ohio, Wilbur and Orville Wright built and repaired bicycles, and used their skills and profits to build the first successful aeroplane.

In India, the bicycle became the vehicle of [[@people-postman-village|postmen]], milkmen, newspaper boys and schoolchildren. Hero Cycles, founded in Ludhiana, [[@punjab|Punjab]], grew into one of the biggest bicycle makers in the world. Many Indian states have given free bicycles to schoolgirls, and a study in Bihar found that more girls enrolled in secondary school after the scheme began.

There are now more than a billion bicycles in the world, and most of them still follow Starley's design from 1885.

text: The Internet of Things, or IoT for short, means everyday objects that connect to the internet and share information. A fitness band that sends your steps to an app is one. So is a smart bulb you switch on from your phone, or a water meter that reports its own reading.

Each one usually has three parts. A [[sensor|sensor]] notices something, such as heat, light, movement or sound. A tiny computer chip makes sense of it. And a wireless link, like [[@wifi|Wi-Fi]] or Bluetooth, sends the information onward, often to an app or a company's computers.

sec.h: The drinks machine that went online
sec.t:
One of the first "things" on a network was a [[@soft-drinks|Coca-Cola machine]] at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. In 1982, students tired of walking to the machine only to find it empty, or the cans still warm. So they wired sensors to it and linked it to the university's computer network. Anyone could type a command and check how many cans were left and how long they had been chilling.

In 1999 a British technology researcher, Kevin Ashton, coined the phrase "Internet of Things" while talking about tags that could track products in shops and warehouses. The name caught on.

IoT reaches far beyond homes. Farmers in India and the USA use sensors buried in fields to measure how wet the soil is, so they water only when crops need it. Water companies fit sensors to pipes to spot leaks. Cities use them to time [[@traffic-lights|traffic lights]], track buses and warn of floods. Hospitals use them to watch patients' [[@heart-beat|heartbeats]] from a nurse's desk.

Planners who design [[@smart-cities|smart cities]] hope that millions of small sensors working together will make streets safer and save water and power.

More connected devices also means more doors for hackers. Many cheap gadgets come with simple default passwords, like "admin", that owners never change.

In 2016 a piece of malicious software called Mirai searched the internet for such devices. It took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers and ordered them all to flood a company that helps run the internet's address system with junk traffic. Popular websites stopped working for hours in parts of the USA and Europe. [[@cybersecurity|Cybersecurity]] experts still use it as a warning.

[[@voice-assistants|A smart speaker]] listens for its wake word. A doorbell camera films the street. A fitness band knows when you sleep. All that data has to be stored somewhere, and people reasonably ask who can see it and how long it is kept.

Countries are starting to set rules. The United Kingdom, for example, banned easy-to-guess default passwords on new [[@smart-homes|smart devices]] from 2024, and the USA has started a label to show which gadgets meet basic security standards.

text: A patent is a legal right, given by a government, that lets an inventor stop anyone else from making, using or selling their invention for a set time, usually 20 years. In return, the inventor must publish a detailed description of how the invention works, so others can learn from it.

To get one, the invention must be new, it must not be obvious to an expert, and it must be useful or able to be made in industry. A patent covers a specific thing, like a new kind of battery or a medicine, not a general wish like "a car that flies". Each country has its own patent office. India's head office is in Kolkata.

st.reveal: A patent is a deal. The government gives you a limited monopoly, usually 20 years, and in return you publish exactly how your invention works. When the patent ends, anyone can use the idea.

sec.h: A deal between inventors and everyone else
sec.t:
Inventing can take years and cost a lot. If anyone could copy a new machine the moment it appeared, inventors might keep their methods secret or not bother at all. A patent offers a reward: a period when only you can sell the invention.

But it comes with a price. You have to explain your invention so clearly that an expert could build it. When the patent runs out, the knowledge belongs to everyone. That's why cheap "generic" medicines appear once a drug's patent expires.

One of the earliest patent laws was passed in [[@venice|Venice]] in 1474. It promised inventors 10 years of protection for new devices. Many other countries later followed. The writers of the US Constitution in 1787 gave Congress the power to grant patents. The first American patent was issued in 1790, for a new way of making potash, used in soap and [[fertiliser|fertiliser]].

[[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] grew up near rivers and had seen boats stuck on sandbanks. In 1849 he patented a system of air-filled floats to lift boats over shallow water. He remains the only US president with a patent.

Sometimes two inventors work on the same thing at once. On 14 February 1876, Alexander Graham Bell's lawyer filed a patent for the telephone on the same day that another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed papers for a similar idea. Bell got the patent, and arguments about who really invented the [[@telephone-history|telephone]] went on in the courts for years.

Thomas Edison held more than a thousand US patents. His long rivalry with [[@nikola-tesla|Nikola Tesla]] and the Westinghouse company over [[@tesla-edison|electricity systems]] was partly a fight over patents and the money they brought.

People argue about whether patents always help. Supporters say they reward invention and get new medicines made. Critics say some patents last too long, keep life-saving drugs expensive in poorer countries, or are granted for tiny tweaks to old products.

India's Patents Act of 1970, updated in 2005, includes a rule against patenting small changes to existing medicines unless they work better. This has helped India become one of the world's biggest makers of affordable generic medicines, though some drug companies have challenged it in court.

text: A modern translation app is a computer program that has studied an enormous number of sentences in two or more languages, side by side. From all those examples it has learned patterns: which words and phrases in one language usually match which in another, and how word order changes.

When you type or speak a sentence, the app turns it into numbers and works out what the whole sentence probably means. Then it builds a new sentence in the other language, word by word. The kind of [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] it uses is called a neural network, loosely inspired by how brain cells connect.

st.prompt: In Turkish and Bengali, the word for "he" and "she" is the same. When early apps translated "She is a doctor" into Bengali and back to English, what often happened?

It came back exactly right every time
The app refused to translate it

st.reveal: The app had no way to know who was meant, so it guessed from patterns in its training text, where doctors were more often written as "he". Researchers spotted this bias, and some apps now show both versions.

d.try: Write three sentences, one plain, one with an idiom like "It's raining cats and dogs", and one joke. Translate each into another language with an app and then back again. Compare the results with the original, and ask someone who speaks that language which version sounds natural.
myth: Translation apps swap words one at a time, like a dictionary.
Modern apps translate whole sentences at once. They look at how every word relates to the others, because word order and meaning change from language to language.

sec.t:
People tried to get machines to translate as early as the 1950s. In 1954 IBM and Georgetown University showed a computer turning about 60 Russian sentences into English. Newspapers predicted perfect translation within a few years.

It took much longer. Early systems used dictionaries and [[@grammar-why|grammar]] rules written by hand. But languages are full of exceptions, [[@idioms|idioms]] and words with many meanings. "Bank" can mean a place for money or the side of a river. Rule-writers could never keep up.

In 2016 Google switched its app to neural translation, and the quality jumped. In 2017 Google researchers described a design called the transformer, which pays "attention" to how every word in a sentence relates to every other word. Transformers now power most translation apps and many chatbots too.

Phones can also translate what they see. The camera reads the letters on a sign, a program recognises them as text, and the translation is drawn over the picture, often in a matching font. Many apps let you download a language pack first, so this works even without an internet connection, which is handy on a mountain trek or a long train journey.

Apps struggle with jokes, poems, slang and idioms. "Break a leg" means good luck in English, but translated literally it sounds alarming. They can also [[@ai-safety|repeat biases]] hidden in their training text, like guessing that a doctor is a man.

Languages with fewer written texts online are harder still. Hindi, [[@bengali-language|Bengali]] and Tamil have hundreds of millions of speakers, but far less digital text than English. Smaller languages, such as many tribal languages of India, may have almost none. That is why some researchers are recording speakers and collecting stories to help [[@endangered-languages|endangered languages]] survive online.

India's [[constitution|constitution]] lists 22 scheduled languages, and many more are spoken. In 2022 the government launched Bhashini, a national mission to build free translation and speech tools for Indian languages. The aim is that a farmer could speak in Odia and be understood by an official who reads only Kannada. Researchers at places like IIT Madras have gathered large collections of Indian-language text and speech to train these systems.

Even so, good [[@translation|human translators]] are still needed for books, courts and hospitals, where a small mistake can matter a lot.

text: Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg developed a new way to print books. He used movable metal letters, oil-based ink and a press adapted from those used for squeezing grapes. A team could now produce hundreds of identical pages a day.

Books became far cheaper and more common. Printing spread to hundreds of European towns within about fifty years. Ideas could travel faster and further than ever. Printed pamphlets helped spread new religious ideas, scientists could share exact drawings and data, and more people had reasons to learn to read. Historians call this the printing revolution.

st.prompt: How many copies of the Gutenberg Bible are thought to survive today, out of around 180 printed?

st.reveal: About 49 copies survive, some complete and some only in parts. They are among the most valuable books in the world, held by libraries such as the Library of Congress in Washington and the British Library in London.

src: British Library, The Diamond Sutra.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, Johannes Gutenberg.
n.certNote: Historians agree that printing spread very fast and changed how ideas travelled. Numbers such as how many books were printed by 1500 are estimates, and scholars still debate how much printing itself caused events like the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.
