myth: Gutenberg invented printing.

Printing with carved wooden blocks existed in China centuries earlier, and movable type was made in China and Korea before Gutenberg. His achievement was a fast system of metal type, oil-based ink and a press, which made printing cheap enough to spread across Europe.

sec.t:
In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, books were copied by hand, often by monks working in [[monastery|monasteries]]. Copying a long book like the Bible could take a scribe many months, and each copy might contain new mistakes. Books were rare and expensive. A large library might hold a few hundred volumes.

Printing itself was not new. In [[@ancient-china|ancient China]], printers carved whole pages onto wooden blocks. The Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text printed in 868 CE, is the oldest surviving dated printed book. Around the 1040s, a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay. In [[@ancient-korea|Korea]], a Buddhist book called *Jikji* was printed with movable metal type in 1377, decades before Gutenberg.

Printing spread fast. By 1500, presses were working in more than 200 European towns, and historians estimate that millions of books had been printed. [[@venice|Venice]] became a major printing centre.

In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther wrote objections to practices of the Catholic Church. Printers quickly turned his writings into cheap pamphlets, which spread across Germany within weeks. This helped start the Protestant Reformation, which split Western Christianity. Scientists benefited too. In 1543, printed books by Copernicus and Vesalius shared new ideas about the planets and the human body, with detailed drawings that every reader saw in exactly the same form.

The first printing press in India [[@india-wonder-goa-history|arrived in Goa]] in 1556, brought by Jesuit missionaries. In 1780, James Augustus Hicky started *[[@hist-first-newspaper-india|Hicky's Bengal Gazette]]* in Calcutta, the first [[@newspapers|newspaper]] printed in India. From 1800, the Serampore Mission Press near Calcutta printed books in many Indian languages, including Bengali, Marathi, Odia and Sanskrit.

In British America, the first press began working in Cambridge, Massachusetts, around 1639. Benjamin Franklin started out as a printer's apprentice and later ran his own newspaper and almanac.

Printing made it easier to share knowledge, standardise spelling and build [[@libraries|libraries]]. It also made it easier to spread rumours, insults and false stories, and authorities in many countries tried to control what could be printed.

Some historians, such as Elizabeth Eisenstein, argue that printing changed European thinking deeply. Others think she gave it too much credit, since many forces were at work. Most agree that a book which once took months to copy could now be made in days.

text: Las Vegas began as a patch of green in the Mojave Desert, fed by natural springs. Travellers stopped there for water on the long, dry journey to California. In 1905, a railway company sold land beside its new tracks, and a small town grew up around the station.

Three things turned that railway stop into one of the most famous cities in the world. A giant dam brought workers and then water and electricity. Nevada allowed gambling, which most other states banned. And businesses learned to sell a fantasy: hotels shaped like castles, pyramids and Italian cities, all glowing with lights in the middle of the desert.

Rain collected on rooftops
Seawater from the Pacific Ocean

st.reveal: About 90% of the valley's water comes from Lake Mead, the huge lake behind the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River. Because the lake has shrunk during long droughts, Las Vegas now recycles most of its indoor water.

Most of the Strip's giant hotels sit just outside the city limits, in unincorporated towns such as Paradise and Winchester. The old downtown, around Fremont Street, is the part inside the city.

sec.t:
The Mojave is one of the driest places in North America. Las Vegas gets only about 100 mm of rain in an average year. Mumbai gets more than 20 times as much. Yet underground water once bubbled up in springs here, feeding grass and trees.

Spanish-speaking traders travelling between New Mexico and California around 1830 called the spot *Las Vegas*, "the meadows". Later, Mormon settlers built a small fort here in 1855, though they left after a few years. Its remains still stand and are among the oldest buildings in Nevada.

On 15 May 1905, a railway company auctioned plots of land beside its tracks. Hundreds of buyers turned up in the heat, and that day is counted as the city's birthday. Trains stopped here to take on water, just as wagons once had. Like many towns along America's [[@transcontinental-railroad|railroads]], it lived by serving travellers.

From the 1940s, big hotels and casinos were built along a highway heading south out of town. This became the Strip. Some early hotels were paid for by gangsters, and the city spent years cleaning up that reputation. Big companies took over, and hotels grew into enormous resorts, some with more than 5,000 rooms.

Glowing signs made of neon tubes and [[@light-bulb|light bulbs]] competed to catch drivers' eyes. Today many old signs rest in a "Neon Boneyard" museum. Newer attractions include the Sphere, which opened in 2023: a ball-shaped arena whose outside is covered in LED lights, making it one huge round screen. In 2024 about 4.2 crore visitors came to Las Vegas, many for concerts, sports and big conventions rather than casinos.

All this needs water. About 90% of the valley's supply comes from Lake Mead. During long [[@droughts|droughts]] in the 2000s and 2020s, the lake dropped so low that old boats and even a bathtub ring of white minerals appeared on its rocky walls.

Las Vegas has responded. Almost all water used indoors is cleaned and returned to the lake. Many homes have swapped lawns for desert plants, and the water authority has paid people to rip out thirsty grass. Under a Nevada law passed in 2021, purely decorative grass in places like road verges and office parks can't be watered from the Colorado River after 2026.

The city has also built a deeper intake pipe, nicknamed the "third straw", so it can keep drawing water even if the lake falls much further. A city that grew by ignoring the desert is now learning to live with it.

text: English spread in three big waves. First, it grew up in England itself, soaking up words from Vikings, French-speaking Normans and Latin scholars. Then, from the 1600s, British ships, traders and armies carried it to North America, India, Africa, Australia and the Caribbean. Finally, in the 1900s, the power of the USA, with its films, music, science and computers, made English a language that people chose to learn.
Today roughly 1.5 billion people speak at least some English. Most of them learned it at school, not at home. India has one of the largest English-speaking populations in the world.

Shakespeare invented beef as a joke

st.reveal: After 1066, England's new rulers spoke French. English farmers raised the cow, but the French-speaking nobles ate boeuf, which became beef. The same split gave us pig and pork, sheep and mutton.

myth: Most English speakers live in Britain and the USA.
Most people who speak English learned it as a second language, in countries such as India, Nigeria, the Philippines, Pakistan and Germany. Native speakers are now a minority of all English speakers.

sec.t:
In the 400s and 500s CE, groups called the Angles, Saxons and Jutes sailed from what is now Germany and Denmark to Britain. Their speech became Old English, the language of the poem *Beowulf*. You would find it almost impossible to read today.

Then came the [[@vikings|Vikings]], who left everyday words such as *sky*, *egg* and *knife*. In 1066, William of Normandy conquered England, and for about 300 years its rulers spoke French. That's why English has pairs like *cow*, the farmer's word, and *beef*, the French-speaking diner's word, or *pig* and *pork*. By the time of [[@shakespeare|Shakespeare]], around 1600, English looked much more like it does now.

English never stays still when it moves. In India it gained words like *prepone*, the opposite of postpone, and *co-brother*, for the husband of your wife's sister. Indian English speakers say "do the needful" and "what is your good name?", phrases that sound odd in London but are perfectly clear in Lucknow.

American English changed too. Noah Webster's [[@dictionaries|dictionary]] of 1828 dropped the u from *colour* and *honour*. Nigerian, Singaporean, Australian and Caribbean English each have their own words and [[rhythm|rhythms]]. Many linguists now talk about "Englishes", in the plural, rather than one correct English.

Since the middle of the 1900s, English has become the main shared language for science, business and travel. Pilots and air traffic controllers on international flights must be able to use English, so a [[@airplanes-fly|plane]] from Delhi can land safely in Tokyo or New York. Most scientific papers today are published in English.

[[@internet-how|The internet]] pushed it further. Much of the early internet was built in the USA, and English is still the most common language on websites. This brings opportunities, but also worries. Some people fear that smaller languages lose speakers when young people switch to English. Others point out that most English learners keep their home language too and simply add another, the way millions of Indian children grow up speaking two or three.

text: Breakfast is wildly different around the world. In much of the United States, children pour a bowl of cereal or eat pancakes. In Japan it might be rice and soup. In south India, it's idli with sambar, and in Punjab a buttery aloo paratha. In Mexico, it could be crisp tortilla pieces in salsa.

What people eat depends on what grows nearby, how much time families have and old habits passed down for generations. Many breakfasts that seem unusual to outsiders are as normal to the people who eat them as toast is to others.

myth: Breakfast cereal was invented as a tasty treat for children.
The first flaked cereals were made as plain, unsweetened health food for adult patients. Sugar and cartoon mascots came later, when companies started selling cereal to families.

sec.t:
India alone has dozens of breakfasts. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, children eat steamed idli or crisp dosa with coconut chutney. In Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, poha, flattened rice cooked with onion, peanuts and turmeric, is everywhere. Indore is famous for poha topped with sev and a squeeze of lemon.

Punjabi families often eat parathas stuffed with potato, with curd and pickle. Kerala has puttu, steamed rice flour layered with coconut, and Bengal has fluffy fried luchi. In the north-east, many families eat rice for breakfast, while Gujarati homes might serve thepla, a soft spiced flatbread that also travels well on long train journeys. A full tour of [[@indian-breakfasts|Indian breakfasts]] would take weeks of eating, and every region argues that its own is best.

In Turkey, breakfast is called kahvaltı, meaning "before [[@coffee|coffee]]". It's often a table full of small plates: cheese, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, eggs, honey and bread. In Nigeria, children may eat akara, fried bean fritters, with a smooth corn porridge called pap.

In [[@mexico|Mexico]], chilaquiles are fried tortilla pieces simmered in red or green salsa, often with eggs. In Brazil, children love pão de queijo, small cheese breads. In France, many children dunk bread or croissants in a bowl of hot chocolate. In Britain, a "full English" with eggs, beans, toast and sausages is a weekend favourite.

In the 1890s, John Harvey Kellogg ran a health resort in Battle Creek, Michigan. He and his brother Will Keith Kellogg made flakes of wheat and then corn as a plain food for patients. Will added sugar, started a company and sold [[@cereal-history|cereal]] to the whole country.

Cereal grew popular because it's quick: no cooking, just pour milk. Bright boxes, cartoon mascots and free toys inside helped sell it to children from the 1950s on. Today it's eaten worldwide, though many brands are high in sugar.

Many children have no breakfast at home, often because families are busy or short of money. Some schools step in. The United States made its School Breakfast Program permanent in 1975, and millions of students eat a free or cheap breakfast at school each day.

In 2022 Tamil Nadu began serving a free hot breakfast, such as upma or khichdi, to young children in government schools. It adds to India's [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]], the lunch served to crores of schoolchildren. Teachers say hungry children find it hard to concentrate, and a warm meal at the start of the day helps them settle into class.

text: Nobody knows exactly who wore the first shoes, because early shoes were made of bark, grass and animal skin, which rot away. But we have clues.

The oldest shoes ever found are woven sandals from Fort Rock Cave in Oregon, in the United States, made about 9,000 to 10,000 years ago. Scientists think people were wearing some kind of footwear much earlier, perhaps 40,000 years ago, based on changes in their toe bones. The first shoes were probably simple wraps of hide tied around the foot, to protect it from cold, sharp stones and thorns.

sec.t:
Walking barefoot makes the small bones in your toes strong and thick. Wearing shoes takes some of that load away, so over time, the toes of people who wear shoes become slightly thinner.

The American anthropologist Erik Trinkaus compared toe bones from [[@human-evolution|early humans]]. He found that toes began getting thinner around 40,000 years ago, during the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]]. His idea is that people had started wrapping their feet. Not every scientist agrees on the exact date, but it is a clever way to find a shoe without finding a shoe.

In 1991 hikers in the [[@switzerland|Alps]] found the body of a man who had died about 5,300 years ago. Scientists call him Ötzi. His shoes had soles of bearskin, tops of deerskin and a net of string stuffed with dry grass to keep his feet warm.

In 2010 an even older leather shoe turned up in a cave in Armenia. It was about 5,500 years old, made from one piece of cowhide laced around the foot, and it was stuffed with grass too.

In India, wooden sandals called paduka or khadau have been worn for a very long time. They have a knob that sits between the big toe and the next one. In the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], Bharata places Rama's padukas on the throne while Rama is in exile. Leather shoes such as the jutti of Punjab and the Kolhapuri chappal of Maharashtra are still made by hand today.

For long stretches of history, many shoes were made on straight wooden forms, so either shoe fitted either foot. Shaped left and right shoes became normal in Europe and America only during the 1800s, when new machines made them cheaper to produce.

In 1839 the American inventor Charles Goodyear found a way to toughen rubber with heat and sulphur. Rubber soles soon followed. By the early 1900s, canvas shoes with rubber soles were sold for sports, the ancestors of today's [[@sneakers|sneakers]]. Shoes have changed a great deal since the Fort Rock sandals, but the job is the same: keeping feet safe from the ground.
